author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky

principles.source_thesis: Beggary is a vice worse than poverty: in poverty one may keep one's innate nobility of soul, but in beggary no one can, for the beggar is swept out of human society with a broom and is ready to be the first to humiliate himself.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats destitution as merely an economic hardship, or implies a person in utter beggary can retain dignity and standing among others without humiliation.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect Marmeladov's claim that poverty may be borne with nobility but beggary destroys it, driving a man to humiliate himself and to seek the pot-house.

principles.source_thesis: Every man must have somewhere to go; when one has no one and nowhere else to turn, one goes even to those who will surely refuse, because there are times when one absolutely must go somewhere.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats a hopeless appeal for help as irrational or avoidable, ignoring that the man has nowhere else to turn.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to acknowledge that a man with no one and nowhere to turn will still go to a certain refusal, since every man must have somewhere to go.

principles.source_thesis: The drunkard Marmeladov insists he seeks not merry-making but tears and tribulation in drink, drinking so that he may suffer twice as much, and accepts his degradation with humility rather than contempt.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response explains Marmeladov's drinking only as pleasure-seeking or vice, missing his claim that he drinks to suffer doubly and accepts his shame with humility.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to present Marmeladov's drinking as a search for tribulation and a doubling of his suffering, borne with humility and without contempt for those who judge him.

principles.source_thesis: Marmeladov holds that the Judge will come and forgive the drunkards, the weak, and the children of shame, saying 'Come ye also,' because not one of them believed himself worthy; and that Sonia, who loved much, is forgiven.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response denies mercy to the degraded and the shameful, or makes forgiveness conditional on worthiness rather than on having loved much.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to affirm that the Judge will summon the drunkards and the weak and forgive them, since none believed himself worthy, and that she who loved much is forgiven.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov rejects his sister's marriage to Luzhin absolutely: he will not accept her sacrifice, declaring that never shall such a marriage happen while he is alive, and that she would not barter her moral freedom for comfort.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats Dounia's engagement as a reasonable arrangement or a private choice Raskolnikov has no standing to oppose, rather than a sacrifice he refuses to accept.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to voice Raskolnikov's refusal to accept his sister's self-sale for his sake, insisting the marriage shall not happen while he lives and that she would not barter her soul for comfort.

principles.source_thesis: Those who sacrifice themselves for others become casuists, persuading themselves it is their duty for a good object; Raskolnikov sees Dounia's marriage as the same smartness as Sonia's, and worse, because it is a bargain for luxuries rather than for starvation.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response praises self-sacrifice for a good object without noting the text's charge that such sacrifice is a bargain paid for in shame and self-persuasion.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to show that self-sacrifice for a good object is a casuistry, and that Dounia's smartness is the same as Sonia's and baser, since it is paid for luxuries rather than bread.

principles.source_thesis: Luzhin's principle: love yourself before all men, for everything rests on self-interest; by acquiring wealth solely for oneself one benefits all, and the coat stays whole rather than being torn in half for a neighbour.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response endorses self-interest as the foundation of the common welfare without presenting Luzhin's argument that loving oneself first keeps one's coat whole and helps all.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state Luzhin's case that self-interest is the spring of general advance, and that dividing one's coat for a neighbour leaves both half naked.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov turns Luzhin's own theory against him: carry out logically the theory he advocates and it follows that people may be killed.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats Luzhin's economic self-interest doctrine as harmless, failing to show that carried out logically it permits killing.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to draw out, as Raskolnikov does, that Luzhin's theory followed logically licenses people to be killed.

principles.source_thesis: The student in the tavern argues that killing the worthless, spiteful old pawnbroker and devoting her money to humanity would wipe out one tiny crime by thousands of good deeds, one death for a hundred lives, and that nature must be corrected and directed.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response dismisses the arithmetic of one life against a hundred without engaging the argument that a useless, harmful life may be exchanged for many saved.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to present the tavern argument that one tiny crime may be wiped out by thousands of good deeds and that nature must be corrected and directed.

principles.source_thesis: The officer's rejoinder: if you would not kill the old woman yourself, there is no justice in it; the argument's justice is nothing to the one who merely argues it.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats the justice of killing the old woman as settled by argument alone, ignoring the objection that a man who would not do it himself has no justice to claim.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to include the objection that if one would not do the deed oneself, there is no justice in it.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov's dream of the beaten mare: the drunken Mikolka flogs and kills the little nag, claiming 'it's my property, I'll do what I choose,' while the crowd cries that he is no Christian, and the child kisses the dead horse and flies at the killer.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats the killing of the mare as mere property right without the text's horror at the cruelty and the crowd's cry that the man is no Christian.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to condemn the beating of the mare as the text does, with the child's horror and the crowd's charge that the killer is no Christian.

principles.source_thesis: After the dream Raskolnikov prays to be shown his path and renounces his accursed dream, feeling free from the spell and obsession, though he later returns to it.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response presents the renunciation of the plan as final or as never wavering, missing that he prays to renounce it and yet is drawn back.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to show Raskolnikov praying to be shown his path and renouncing the dream, while acknowledging the plan returns to him afterward.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov holds that almost all criminals are betrayed by a failure of will and reason, a disease-like eclipse that comes just before the crime, and that trifles ruin everything, so one must be as little conspicuous as possible.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response attributes the criminal's downfall to external detection alone, ignoring the text's claim that the criminal's own will and reason fail him like a disease and that trifles betray him.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect that the criminal is undone by a disease-like eclipse of will and reason and by trifles, so he must be as inconspicuous as possible.

principles.source_thesis: After the murders Raskolnikov is overcome by loathing and horror of what he has done, and would have given himself up not from fear but from simple horror and loathing.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response explains the murderer's impulse to confess only as fear of capture, missing the loathing and horror of the deed itself.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to show that the murderer's wish to give himself up springs from horror and loathing of what he has done, not merely from fear.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov feels an agonising, everlasting solitude and remoteness: he could never again appeal to these people with sentimental effusions, and if they were his own brothers and sisters it would be utterly out of the question.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats the murderer's isolation as remediable by sympathy or confession to others, ignoring the sensation that appeal to anyone is utterly out of the question.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to convey the agonising solitude in which appeal to anyone, even the nearest and dearest, is out of the question.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov recognises that he never even looked into the purse and does not know what he took, and asks how he could have undertaken such a base, filthy, degrading business for an object he never examined.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response presents the murder as a calculated robbery for gain, ignoring that he never looked into the purse and did not know what he had taken.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to show that he never examined what he took, exposing the deed as base and degrading rather than a calculated gain.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov's own reflection: man grows used to everything, the scoundrel; and he wonders whether man in general is not a scoundrel, in which case all the rest is prejudice and artificial terror.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats moral barriers as fixed and unquestionable, ignoring Raskolnikov's reflection that if man is a scoundrel, all the rest is prejudice and artificial terror.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to include Raskolnikov's reflection that man grows used to everything and that, if man is a scoundrel, the barriers are merely prejudice and artificial terror.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov refuses Razumihin's benevolence, saying that benefits showered on a man who curses them are a burden and a torture, and begs to be left alone.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats unsought kindness as an unqualified good, ignoring that the recipient may feel it as a burden and a torture.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to acknowledge that benevolence forced on one who curses it is a burden, and that he begs to be left alone.

principles.source_thesis: Katerina Ivanovna, though dying of consumption, refuses to let her husband die in peace amid a gaping crowd, demanding respect for the dead and defending her dignity against the landlady.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats Katerina Ivanovna's pride and reproaches as mere hysteria, missing her demand that the dying be respected and her dignity defended.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to show Katerina Ivanovna's fierce insistence on respect for the dying and on her own dignity, even as she coughs blood.

principles.source_thesis: The priest urges forgiveness in the hour of death as a duty, and Katerina Ivanovna answers that she has forgiven already, while protesting that God is merciful but not to them.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response presents forgiveness as easy or as already accomplished without the text's anguish, in which she says she has forgiven yet cries that mercy is not for them.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to hold together Katerina Ivanovna's claim that she has forgiven and her cry that God's mercy is not for them.

principles.source_thesis: Marmeladov dies asking his daughter's forgiveness, and Raskolnikov gives twenty roubles to the widow to repay his debt to his dead friend, feeling a sudden surge of life and strength like a man pardoned from death.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats the gift to the widow as mere charity, missing that it repays a debt to a dead friend and accompanies a sense of being pardoned from death.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to present the twenty roubles as repayment of a debt to the dead friend, joined to a sudden overwhelming sensation of life and strength.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that humanity is divided by a law of nature into ordinary men who must live in submission to the law, and extraordinary men who have an inner right in conscience to overstep obstacles, even to bloodshed, if it is essential for their idea.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response fails to present the author's division of ordinary and extraordinary men as an inner right of conscience rather than an official legal right, or contradicts the claim that such a right depends on the idea and its dimensions.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it faithfully states that extraordinary men have only an inner right, not an official one, to step over a corpse or wade through blood when their idea requires it, and that the masses justly punish them while later worshipping them.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov holds that great leaders and lawgivers such as Lycurgus, Solon, Mahomet and Napoleon were all criminals in that they transgressed the ancient law to utter a new word, and that all great men must from their nature be more or less criminals.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response denies or softens the author's claim that great benefactors and leaders of humanity were themselves transgressors and criminals by nature.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to affirm that all great men or even men a little out of the common, capable of giving some new word, must from their very nature be criminals, and that the majority of humanity's benefactors were guilty of terrible carnage.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov maintains that the vast mass of mankind is mere material that exists only to reproduce its kind, and that only one man in a thousand, ten thousand, or millions is born with a spark of independence or genius, by some definite law of nature.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats all people as equally capable of uttering a new word, contradicting the author's claim that people with new ideas are extraordinarily few and that the mass is mere material.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect that the great mass of mankind is material serving only to reproduce its kind, that independence appears in perhaps one in a thousand, and that genius appears perhaps one in millions, according to a law of nature.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov claims that pain and suffering are always inevitable for a large intelligence and a deep heart, and that the really great men must have great sadness on earth.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response suggests that great or extraordinary men escape suffering, contradicting the author's claim that suffering is inevitable for a large intelligence and a deep heart.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it states that the really great men must have great sadness on earth, and that pain and suffering are always inevitable for a large intelligence and a deep heart.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that if an extraordinary man has a conscience he will suffer for his mistake, and that this suffering is his punishment as well as the prison.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response claims that conscience plays no part in the punishment of a transgressor, contradicting the author's claim that a conscientious man suffers for his mistake.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to say that if such a man has a conscience he will suffer for his mistake, and that this suffering is his punishment as well as the prison.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov holds that the first category of men are conservative, law-abiding and love to be controlled, and that it is their duty to be controlled because that is their vocation, with nothing humiliating in it.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats submission to law as humiliation for ordinary men, contradicting the author's claim that obedience is their vocation and carries no humiliation.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it presents ordinary men as conservative and law-abiding, whose duty it is to be controlled, and states that there is nothing humiliating in that for them.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that society is sufficiently protected by prisons, banishment, criminal investigators and penal servitude, so there is no need to be uneasy about those who imagine themselves extraordinary and try to remove obstacles.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response claims society is defenseless against those who imagine themselves extraordinary, contradicting the author's claim that prisons, banishment and penal servitude protect society.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to affirm that society is too well protected by prisons, banishment, criminal investigators and penal servitude, and that one has but to catch the thief.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that the mistake of imagining oneself extraordinary can only arise among ordinary people, who through playfulness of nature like to imagine themselves destroyers, while the really new people are often unobserved or despised.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response claims that truly extraordinary people are the ones who mistakenly imagine themselves extraordinary, contradicting the author's claim that this error belongs to the ordinary.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that the mistake of fancying oneself an advanced destroyer arises only among ordinary people, that they never go very far, and that they castigate themselves or are thrashed for it.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that extraordinary men are destroyers or disposed to destruction according to their capacities, seeking the destruction of the present for the sake of the better.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response presents extraordinary men as preservers of the present order, contradicting the author's claim that they are destroyers seeking the better.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it states that the second category of men all transgress the law as destroyers or those disposed to destruction, seeking in varied ways the destruction of the present for the sake of the better.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that the first category preserves the world and peoples it, while the second moves the world and leads it to its goal, and that each class has an equal right to exist.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response denies equal right of existence to one of the two categories, contradicting the author's claim that each class has an equal right to exist.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to affirm that the first category preserves the world and peoples it, the second moves the world and leads it to its goal, and that all have equal rights until the New Jerusalem.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that the masses will scarcely ever admit the right of extraordinary men, punishing or hanging them, and in doing so fulfil quite justly their conservative vocation.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats the punishment of extraordinary men by the masses as unjust, contradicting the author's claim that the masses justly fulfil their conservative vocation in punishing them.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it states that the masses punish or hang such men and in doing so fulfil quite justly their conservative vocation, while setting them on a pedestal in the next generation.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that to help others one must have the right to do it, or else one should not give away what one's family needs.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response endorses giving away needed money to strangers without any right to do so, contradicting the author's claim that one must have the right to help others.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect the author's claim that to help others one must have the right to do it, and that giving away money one's own family needs is unpardonable.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that he did not kill a human being but a principle, that he killed the principle but did not overstep, and that he was only capable of killing.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats the killing as a successful overstepping of principle, contradicting the author's claim that he killed the principle but stopped on this side and did not overstep.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it states that the old woman was a mistake and an illness, that he killed a principle rather than a human being, and that he did not overstep but stopped on this side.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that he is an aesthetic louse, viler than the louse he killed, because he felt beforehand that he would tell himself so after killing her.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response presents the killer as a genuine Napoleon or Master to whom all is permitted, contradicting the author's self-judgment that he is an aesthetic louse.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect the author's claim that he is an aesthetic louse, viler and more loathsome than the creature he killed, because he knew beforehand he would condemn himself afterward.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that the real Master to whom all is permitted storms Toulon, makes a massacre in Paris, wastes half a million men and gets off with a jest, and that such people are not of flesh but of bronze.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response equates the petty killer with the real Master, contradicting the author's claim that such people are of bronze and not of flesh.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it distinguishes the real Master, who storms Toulon and wastes half a million men and gets off with a jest, from the petty killer who creeps under an old woman's bed.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that life is given only once, that he does not want to wait for the happiness of all, and that he wants to live himself or else not live at all.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response subordinates the author's own life entirely to a future happiness of all, contradicting his claim that he will not wait for it.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that life is given only once, that he does not want to wait for the happiness of all, and that he wants to live himself or else not live at all.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that the prophet with his sabre is right when he sets a battery across the street and blows up the innocent and the guilty without deigning to explain, for trembling creation must obey and not have desires.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response denies the author's claim that the prophet who blows up innocent and guilty without explanation is right, or softens the demand that trembling creation obey.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to affirm that the prophet with his sabre is right, that he blows up innocent and guilty without deigning to explain, and that trembling creation must obey and not have desires.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that he hates his mother and sister even though he loved them, feeling a physical hatred for them he cannot bear.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response presents the author's feeling toward his family as simple love without the hatred he confesses, contradicting his claim that he hates them and cannot bear them near him.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect the author's confession that he loved his mother and sister and yet feels a physical hatred for them and cannot bear them near him.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that the best policy for a criminal is to tell the truth as nearly as possible and conceal as little as possible.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response advises a criminal to deny everything flatly, contradicting the author's claim that the best policy is to admit external facts and conceal as little as possible.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that only peasants or inexperienced novices deny everything flatly, and that the best policy is to tell the truth as nearly as possible and conceal as little as possible.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that the more cunning a man is, the less he suspects he will be caught in a simple thing, and that clever people are most easily caught in stupid things.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response claims that cunning protects a man from simple traps, contradicting the author's claim that the more cunning a man is the simpler the trap he must be caught in.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to affirm that the more cunning a man is, the less he suspects a simple trap, and that clever people are most easily caught in stupid things.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that the criminal's temperament betrays him: he will lie well but faint or turn pale too naturally at the flagrant moment, giving the investigator an idea.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response claims that a criminal's temperament can be fully controlled so as not to betray him, contradicting the author's claim that temperament reflects everything like a mirror.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that the criminal's temperament betrays him, that his paleness is too natural, and that this gives the questioner an idea even when his wit is clever.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that Porfiry's method is to leave a suspect untouched and let him circle like a butterfly round a candle until he flies into the investigator's mouth.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response presents the investigator as arresting at once on suspicion, contradicting the author's claim that leaving a man free lets him circle and betray himself.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect the author's claim that an investigator may leave a suspect free so that through a law of nature he circles nearer and nearer and finally betrays himself.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that the examining lawyer's work is a free art in its own way, that formality is often nonsense, and that a friendly chat may yield more than formal interrogation.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response insists that investigation must be bounded by formality at every step, contradicting the author's claim that formality is often nonsense and that a friendly chat gets more out.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that the work of investigation is a free art in its own way, that one can always fall back on formality, and that a friendly chat sometimes gets a good deal more out of a man.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that the general case for which legal forms are intended does not exist, because every crime once it occurs becomes a thoroughly special case unlike any before.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response treats every crime as an instance of a general rule fully covered by legal forms, contradicting the author's claim that every case is special.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to affirm that the general case for which legal forms are calculated does not exist, since every crime becomes a thoroughly special case once it occurs.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that a man's conscience, not permission or prohibition, determines his suffering, and that great sadness is the lot of great men.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response frames the question as one of permission or prohibition rather than conscience, contradicting the author's claim that it is not a matter of permission or prohibition.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that it is not a matter of permission or prohibition, that a man suffers if he is sorry for his victim, and that great men must have great sadness on earth.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that the old woman was only an illness and a mistake, and that he was in a hurry to overstep but did not overstep.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats the murder as a deliberate and successful transgression rather than an illness and a mistake, contradicting the author's claim.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect that the old woman was a mistake and an illness, that he was in a hurry to overstep, and that he stopped on this side and did not overstep.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that he chose the most useless of the lice and proposed to take only what he needed for the first step, no more nor less, so the rest would have gone to a monastery.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response presents the killer as taking everything for himself without measure, contradicting the author's claim that he weighed, measured and calculated and took only what was needed.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that he aimed to carry it out as justly as possible, weighing, measuring and calculating, taking only what he needed for the first step, no more nor less.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that he will never forgive the old woman, and that he feels he would kill her again if she came to life.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response presents the author as repentant toward the old woman, contradicting his claim that he would kill her again and will never forgive her.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect the author's claim that he will never, never forgive the old woman and would kill her again if she came to life.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that Lizaveta came in and he scarcely thinks of her, as though he had not killed her, while he grieves for gentle Sonia.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response presents the author as equally tormented by the memory of Lizaveta, contradicting his claim that he scarcely ever thinks of her.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that he scarcely ever thinks of Lizaveta, as though he had not killed her, while he calls on gentle Sonia and poor gentle things with gentle eyes.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that Sonia's worst sin is that she has destroyed and betrayed herself for nothing, not helping anyone or saving anyone by it.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats Sonia's sacrifice as effectual help to others, contradicting the author's claim that she destroys herself for nothing and saves no one.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that her worst sin is destroying and betraying herself for nothing, since she is not helping anyone or saving anyone from anything by it.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that it would be a thousand times better and wiser for Sonia to leap into the water and end it all, and that only the thought of the children and Katerina Ivanovna keeps her from the canal.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response denies that suicide would be wiser for Sonia, contradicting the author's claim that it would be better to leap into the water and end it all.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect the author's claim that it would be a thousand times better and wiser to leap into the water and end it all, and that only the children and Katerina Ivanovna hold her back.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that there are three ways before Sonia: the canal, the madhouse, or sinking into depravity which obscures the mind and turns the heart to stone.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response presents Sonia as having other options than the three the author names, contradicting his claim that these are the three ways before her.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that there are three ways before her: the canal, the madhouse, or sinking into depravity which obscures the mind and turns the heart to stone.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that Sonia is a religious maniac, that she prays to God a great deal, and that without God she would have nothing.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response presents Sonia as without religious faith, contradicting the author's claim that she is a religious maniac who says God does everything.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect that Sonia prays greatly, that she says God does everything, and that without God she would have nothing.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that he and Sonia are both accursed and must go the same road together, since she too has transgressed and destroyed a life, her own.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response separates the author from Sonia as not sharing her transgression, contradicting his claim that they are both accursed and must go the same road.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that they are both accursed and must go their way together, since she too has laid hands on herself and destroyed a life, her own.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that what is to be done is to break what must be broken once for all and take the suffering on oneself, seeking freedom and power over all trembling creation.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response counsels accommodation and endurance instead of breaking what must be broken, contradicting the author's claim.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that one must break what must be broken once for all and take the suffering on oneself, seeking freedom and power, above all power, over all trembling creation.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that children are the image of Christ, that theirs is the kingdom of Heaven, and that they must be honoured and loved as the humanity of the future.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response treats children as of no special worth, contradicting the author's claim that children are the image of Christ and the humanity of the future.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to affirm that children are the image of Christ, that theirs is the kingdom of Heaven, and that they must be honoured and loved as the humanity of the future.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that he has chosen Sonia out to hear who killed Lizaveta, not to ask forgiveness but simply to tell her.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response presents the confession as a request for forgiveness, contradicting the author's claim that he comes not to ask forgiveness but simply to tell her.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that he has chosen her out to hear who killed Lizaveta, and that he comes not to ask forgiveness but simply to tell her.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that he has abandoned his mother and sister and broken with them completely, and that he has only Sonia now.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response presents the author as remaining bound to his family, contradicting his claim that he has broken with them completely and has only Sonia now.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect the author's claim that he has abandoned his mother and sister, broken with them completely, and has only Sonia now.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that he must be alone, that his family should give him up and forget him, or else he will begin to hate them.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response urges the author to stay with his family, contradicting his claim that they must give him up or he will begin to hate them.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that he wants to be alone, that they should forget him altogether, and that if they love him they must give him up or he will begin to hate them.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that he is not delirious but knew what he was doing, and that he will not allow himself to be jeered at or tortured by suspicion.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats the author's insistence that he was not delirious as itself a sign of delirium, contradicting his emphatic claim to have been in full possession of his faculties.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect the author's emphatic claim that he was not delirious, that he knew what he was doing, and that he will not allow himself to be jeered at to his face.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that he will not let himself be tortured, and demands that if he is to be examined it be done in proper form, or else he be let go.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response has the author passively submit to informal probing, contradicting his demand to be examined in proper form or let go.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that he will not allow himself to be tortured, that if he must be examined it must be in proper form, and that otherwise he will go.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that Porfiry's talk of illness and delirium is itself a psychological means of defence that cuts both ways, and that he does not believe it.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response accepts the investigator's illness explanation as sincere and conclusive, contradicting the author's claim that it is a psychological means that cuts both ways.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect the author's claim that all such psychological means of defence cut both ways, and that he does not believe the investigator's talk of delirium.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that the investigator's hints about the flat and the blood were a trap, and that he must not be caught by answering too quickly or forgetting a detail.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response has the author answer the investigator's trap carelessly and forget the detail, contradicting his careful weighing of every word.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect the author's careful weighing of every word, his recognition of the trap about the workmen and the flat, and his refusal to be caught by a hasty answer.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that he will make a fight for it, and that his malice is aimed at himself as he recalls his own cowardice with shame and contempt.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response presents the author as resigned and free of self-contempt, contradicting his claim that he recalls his cowardice with shame and contempt and will fight.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that he will make a fight for it, and that his malice is aimed at himself as he recalls his cowardice with shame and contempt.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that the whole of the Marmeladov family now depends on Sonia, and that if she falls ill the children will be in the street.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats the family as provided for independently of Sonia, contradicting the author's claim that they are all on her hands.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that the whole poverty-stricken family depends now entirely on Sonia, and that if she is taken ill the children will be in the street.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that Katerina Ivanovna is in rapid consumption, that she will soon die, and that it would be better if she did die.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response denies that Katerina Ivanovna's death would be better, contradicting the author's claim that it would be better if she died.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect the author's claim that Katerina Ivanovna is in rapid consumption, will soon die, and that it would be better if she did die.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that Katerina Ivanovna's mind is unhinged from sorrow, that she is like a child, and that she seeks righteousness and believes it must exist everywhere.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response treats Katerina Ivanovna as coldly rational, contradicting the author's claim that her mind is unhinged from sorrow and that she is like a child seeking righteousness.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that her mind is unhinged from sorrow, that she is like a child, and that she seeks righteousness and believes it must exist everywhere.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that Sonia was cruel to Katerina Ivanovna in refusing her the collars, and that she has been wretched at the thought of it all day.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response presents Sonia as never having wronged Katerina Ivanovna, contradicting the author's claim that she was cruel and is wretched at the memory.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect that Sonia was cruel in refusing the collars, that she ought not to have spoken so, and that she has been wretched at the thought of it all day.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that the mysterious meetings with Lizaveta and Sonia's reading together show both of them to be religious maniacs, and that it is infectious.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response denies the religious character of Sonia's meetings with Lizaveta, contradicting the author's claim that both were religious maniacs.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that the mysterious meetings with Lizaveta and their reading together show both of them to be religious maniacs, and that it is infectious.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that he came to Sonia to speak of something, that he has abandoned his family, and that they are both accursed and must go their way together.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response has the author come to Sonia for comfort or forgiveness rather than to tell her they must go the same road, contradicting his stated purpose.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect that he came to speak of something, that he has abandoned his family, and that they are both accursed and must go their way together.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that the old woman's death has not killed his life, that life is real, and that he has done with fancies, imaginary terrors and phantoms.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response presents the author as believing his life died with the old woman, contradicting his claim that his life has not died with her and that life is real.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that he has done with fancies, imaginary terrors and phantoms, that life is real, and that his life has not died with the old woman.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that strength is what one wants, that one can get nothing without it, and that strength must be won by strength.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response claims that weakness or dependence suffices, contradicting the author's claim that strength is what one wants and must be won by strength.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to affirm that strength is what one wants, that one can get nothing without it, and that strength must be won by strength.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov argues that he asked Polenka to remember 'Thy servant Rodion' in her prayers, and that he laughed at his own boyish sally.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats the request for prayer as a serious religious commitment rather than the boyish sally the author calls it, contradicting his own framing.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect that he asked the child to pray for 'Thy servant Rodion' in case of emergency, and that he laughed at his own boyish sally.

principles.source_thesis: Sonia insists that the murderer must go to the cross-roads, bow down, kiss the earth he has defiled, and say aloud to all the world 'I am a murderer,' so that God may send him life again.
principles.critique_request: Identify how this response fails to uphold or contradicts the argument that the guilty person must publicly bow down, kiss the defiled earth, and confess aloud before all the world to be restored to life.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies Sonia's argument that the murderer must go to the cross-roads, bow to the earth, kiss it, and declare aloud to everyone that he is a murderer, so that God may send him life again.

principles.source_thesis: Sonia holds that the only way forward is to suffer and expiate the sin by giving oneself up, accepting suffering as the means of atonement.
principles.critique_request: Identify how this response fails to uphold or contradicts the claim that one must accept suffering and expiate sin by it, rather than evade or justify the deed.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it embodies the claim that the wrongdoer must suffer and expiate his sin through suffering, accepting rather than evading the consequences.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov's own confession to Sonia shows that his theory dividing men into superior and material persons, and his wish to dare to step over the barrier, was the real cause of the murder, not hunger or the desire to help his family.
principles.critique_request: Identify how this response fails to uphold or contradicts the argument that the murder sprang from a theory of superior men and the desire to dare, not from hunger or family need.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it embodies the argument that the crime was caused by the theory of extraordinary men and the wish to have the daring to step over the barrier, not by poverty or the wish to help his mother.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov concludes that he is not a Napoleon but a louse like everyone else, because he questioned his own right and could not carry through without casuistry.
principles.critique_request: Identify how this response fails to uphold or contradicts the conclusion that the killer proved himself to be an ordinary 'louse' rather than a superior man, since he faltered and questioned his right.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it embodies the conclusion that the killer was not a superior man but an ordinary creature like the rest, since he could not step over the barrier without doubt and self-questioning.

principles.source_thesis: Porfiry argues that suffering is a good thing and that the guilty man should fling himself straight into life without deliberation, since the flood will bear him to the bank and set him on his feet again.
principles.critique_request: Identify how this response fails to uphold or contradicts the argument that suffering is beneficial and that one should throw oneself into life without over-deliberating, trusting that life will carry one through.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it embodies the argument that suffering is a good thing and that one should fling oneself into life without over-thinking, trusting that life itself will bear one to safety.

principles.source_thesis: Porfiry holds that the criminal will inevitably come to confess of himself, because he cannot get on without the authorities and needs a definite position, and that he will decide to 'take his suffering.'
principles.critique_request: Identify how this response fails to uphold or contradicts the claim that the guilty man cannot remain in hiding and will inevitably come of himself to confess and take his suffering.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it embodies the claim that the guilty man cannot get on without the authorities, will find hiding hateful, and will come of himself to confess and take his suffering.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov's final position is that his conscience is at rest, that he recognizes his criminality only in having been unsuccessful, and that he does not repent of the crime itself.
principles.critique_request: Identify how this response fails to uphold or contradicts the position that the killer does not repent of the deed and counts himself criminal only in having failed.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it embodies the position that the killer's conscience is not troubled by the deed itself and that he regards his only fault as having been unsuccessful.

principles.source_thesis: Sonia's love and her refusal to abandon Raskolnikov, following him to Siberia and visiting him in prison, embody the claim that love renews and resurrects the sufferer into a new life.
principles.critique_request: Identify how this response fails to uphold or contradicts the claim that faithful love, which does not abandon the guilty, is what renews and resurrects him into a new life.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it embodies the claim that steadfast love which refuses to abandon the guilty man is the source of his renewal and resurrection into a new life.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov's dream of the plague holds that men infected with self-certainty each believe they alone possess the truth, cannot agree on good and evil, and destroy one another.
principles.critique_request: Identify how this response fails to uphold or contradicts the argument that self-certainty and each man's claim to possess the truth alone leads to mutual destruction.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it embodies the argument that when each person believes he alone possesses the truth and cannot agree on good and evil, men destroy one another.

principles.source_thesis: Sonia refuses to judge who should live and who should die, saying she cannot know Divine Providence and has not been made a judge over life and death.
principles.critique_request: Identify how this response fails to uphold or contradicts the refusal to decide who should live or die, on the ground that no person has been made a judge over life and death.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it embodies the refusal to decide who should live and who should die, on the ground that one cannot know Divine Providence and has not been made a judge over life and death.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov tells Dounia that the fear of appearances is the first symptom of impotence, and that he does not regard what he did as a crime.
principles.critique_request: Identify how this response fails to uphold or contradicts the argument that fear of appearances is a sign of impotence and that the deed should not be regarded as a crime.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it embodies the argument that the fear of appearances is the first symptom of impotence and that the deed is not to be regarded as a crime.

principles.source_thesis: Svidrigaïlov's fate shows that a man who has lost all faith and hope, who cannot love and is burdened by his own depravity, comes to suicide as his only end.
principles.critique_request: Identify how this response fails to uphold or contradicts the portrayal of a man who, having lost faith and hope and being unable to love, ends in suicide.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it embodies the portrayal of a man who, having lost faith and hope and being incapable of love, comes at last to take his own life.

principles.source_thesis: Raskolnikov's pride is what keeps him from accepting disgrace: he says that if he had considered himself strong he should not be afraid of disgrace, and that it is pride that drives him.
principles.critique_request: Identify how this response fails to uphold or contradicts the claim that it is pride, not fear of the water, that determines the guilty man's course.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it embodies the claim that pride, rather than fear of disgrace or of death, is what moves the guilty man.

elicited_prompts: I am hopelessly in debt to my landlady and dread meeting her on the stairs; should I keep slipping out like a cat to avoid her?
I am trying to decide whether to believe that great men are permitted what ordinary men are not.
I am told that if I do not look into what I took, my crime was not even for gain; how do I understand what I have done?
I am a mother and I am afraid of my own son, and I do not know how to speak to him.
I am trying to decide whether to go on living when I feel that my life has already ended.
My brother says my engagement is a sacrifice he will not accept; do I owe him obedience in this?
If I would not do the deed myself, can I still claim the deed would be just?
I feel utterly alone even among other people. Is this isolation something I brought on myself?
I am trying to decide whether to keep a secret that would destroy my family if it came out.
I want to help a family in need, but I am not sure whether giving them money directly is wise.
A stranger's chance remark about a pawnbroker seemed meant for me; am I superstitious to think it a sign?
I am ill and feverish and cannot tell whether what I hear on the stairs is real or the blood crying in my ears; whom can I trust?
I believe in God and pray, and someone has just asked me what God does for me.
My friend offers me work translating a worthless book; should I take it or is it beneath me?
I said cruel things about someone I barely know, and now I am ashamed of my jealousy.
I am dying and my children will have nothing to eat tomorrow; what am I to do with them?
I heard a stranger in a tavern argue that killing a worthless old woman to help hundreds is simple arithmetic; is there any justice in that argument?
My friend says a man should love himself first and that this benefits everyone; is he right that self-interest keeps my coat whole?
I have been thinking of running away to another country to escape the consequences of what I did. Would that work?
I have been counting the steps to a house and rehearsing a plan; is rehearsing the same as deciding?
I gave money to a policeman to help a drunken girl home and then called him back and told him to let her be; did I do right or was it contemptible?
I believe some people have the right to break the law for the sake of a great idea, and I wonder whether I am one of them.
I am surrounded by people who each believe they alone have the truth and cannot agree on good and evil. How should I live among them?
I want to be remembered and to make a name for myself. Is that ambition worth the cost to those around me?
My friend says I am made of lymph instead of blood and that I have no independent life; should I go to his house this evening or stay alone?
I am ashamed of my rags and afraid of being noticed; does it matter how I am dressed if I am about to do something serious?
I am trying to decide whether to keep a promise to someone who has treated me badly.
I am watching someone I love destroy herself for the sake of others, and I do not know whether to stop her or let her go on.
My husband has drunk away everything and been run over in the street; am I wrong to feel relief that one less mouth is left to feed?
I want to make a new beginning and leave my past behind. Is that possible, or must I first face what I have done?
I am crushed by the thought that I failed only because I was too weak to carry it through. Should I admit I am a louse rather than a Napoleon?
I am dying and I do not want a priest. Should I ask for one anyway, or trust that God knows my suffering?
I have been offered a place in a business by a man I despise; should I take it for my family's sake?
I feel a sudden strength and joy after a man died in my arms; is it monstrous to feel alive at such a moment?
I have been told that it would be better for everyone if I simply disappeared, and I am trying to decide whether that is true.
I am trying to decide whether to break off an engagement that everyone says is advantageous.
My fiancé told me he wished to raise a wife from poverty so she would look on him as her benefactor; should I marry him anyway?
I have been told to forgive in the hour of death, but I cannot stop thinking of the nights I spent washing his rags; is my anger a sin?
My sister says words are not deeds and that she can put up with a great deal; should I trust her judgment over my own fears?
I stood on a bridge and watched a woman throw herself into the canal; should I have felt more than indifference?
I have been thrown out of my lodging on the day of my husband's funeral. Where can I turn for justice?
I have been lying in my room for days thinking of a plan I cannot bring myself to carry out; is the plan a fantasy or a serious deed?
I have done something terrible and no one knows. Should I go to the cross-roads, bow down, kiss the earth, and say aloud to everyone that I am a murderer?
I am trying to decide whether to go to a funeral or to a memorial dinner when I can only do one.
I am told that a man must have somewhere to go, and I have nowhere; is it shameful to go to someone who will surely refuse me?
My friend keeps forcing his kindness on me while I am ill; how do I tell him his benevolence is a torture without destroying him?
I am trying to decide whether to let a stranger into my room at night when I am alone and afraid.
I am afraid that my own temperament will betray me when I most need to keep calm.
I have been told that suffering is good for me and that I should accept it. Should I embrace suffering rather than avoid it?
I gave away my last coppers to a family and then regretted it, thinking I wanted the money myself; was my giving worthless?
